etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English hoste, from Old French oste (French: hôte), from Latin hospitem, accusative of hospes (“a host, also a sojourner, visitor, guest; hence, a foreigner, a stranger”), from *hostipotis, an old compound of hostis and the root of potis, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰostipotis (“master of guests”), from *gʰóstis (“stranger, guest, enemy”) and *pótis (“owner, master, host, husband”). Used in English since 13th century.

definitions.definition: One which receives or entertains a guest, socially, commercially, or officially.

quote.citation: c. 1602, William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Troylus and Cressida”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene iii]:
quote.text: Time is like a fashionable host, / That slightly shakes his parting guest by the hand.

definitions.definition: One that provides a facility for an event.
A person or organization responsible for running an event.
A moderator or master of ceremonies for a performance.
(computing, Internet) Any computer attached to a network.
(ecology) A cell or organism which harbors another organism or biological entity, usually a parasite.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, Katie L. Burke, “In the News”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3, page 193:
quote.text: A recent study explored the ecological variables that may contribute to bats’ propensity to harbor such zoonotic diseases by comparing them with another order of common reservoir hosts: rodents.

definitions.definition: (evolution, genetics) An organism bearing certain genetic material, with respect to its cells.
A paid male companion offering conversation and in some cases sex, as in certain types of bar in Japan.
To perform the role of a host.

quote.citation: 2013 May-June, Katie L. Burke, “In the News”, in American Scientist, volume 101, number 3, page 193:
quote.text: Bats host many high-profile viruses that can infect humans, including severe acute respiratory syndrome and Ebola.

definitions.definition: (obsolete, intransitive) To lodge at an inn.

quote.citation: c. 1604–1605 (date written), William Shakespeare, “All’s Well, that Ends Well”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act III, scene v]:

definitions.definition: (computing, Internet) To run software made available to a remote user or process.

quote.citation: 1987 May 7, Selden E. Ball, Jr., “Re: Ethernet Terminal Concentrators”, in comp.protocols.tcp-ip (Usenet):
quote.text: CMU/TEK TCP/IP software uses an excessive amount of cpu resources for terminal support both outbound, when accessing another system, and inbound, when the local system is hosting a session.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English oost, borrowed from Old French ost, oste, hoste, from Latin hostis (“foreign enemy”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰóstis (as opposed to inimicus (“personal enemy”)). Doublet of guest.

definitions.definition: A multitude of people arrayed as an army; used also in religious senses, as: Heavenly host (of angels)

quote.citation: 1843 April, Thomas Carlyle, “ch. X, Plugson of Undershot”, in Past and Present, American edition, Boston, Mass.: Charles C[offin] Little and James Brown, published 1843, →OCLC, book III (The Modern Worker):
quote.text: Why, Plugson, even thy own host is all in mutiny: Cotton is conquered; but the ‘bare backs’ — are worse covered than ever!

quote.citation: 1955 October 20, J[ohn] R[onald] R[euel] Tolkien, “chapter 4, The Field of Cormallen”, in The Return of the King: Being the Third Part of The Lord of the Rings […], New York, N.Y.: Ballantine Books, published December 1978, →ISBN:
quote.text: All about the hosts of Mordor raged.

quote.citation: 1977, K.M. Elizabeth Murray, Caught in the Web of Words, Oxford: Oxford University Press, page 173:
quote.text: By Lady Day the Scriptorium was ready to receive the "copying and burrowing" of the host of readers who had been directed by Furnivall for the past twenty years.

quote.citation: 2001, Carlos Parada, Hesione 2, Greek Mythology Link:
quote.text: the invading host that had sailed from Hellas in more than one thousand ships was of an unprecedented size.

definitions.definition: A large number of items; a large inventory.

quote.citation: 1802, William Wordsworth, I Wandered Lonely as a Cloud:
quote.text: I wandered lonely as a cloudThat floats on high o'er vales and hills,When all at once I saw a crowd,A host, of golden daffodils;  […]

quote.citation: 1836, The Mirror of Literature, Amusement, and Instruction:
quote.text: A short time since, some friends drinking tea one summer evening at their residence near Maidenhead, with all the windows of the drawing-room open, there suddenly burst in a host of small flies, which covered the table and the furniture  […]

quote.citation: 2018 June 18, Phil McNulty, “Tunisia 1 – 2 England”, in BBC Sport‎[1], archived from the original on 21 April 2019:
quote.text: England ran Tunisia ragged in that spell but were punished for missing a host of chances when Ferjani Sassi equalised from the penalty spot against the run of play after Kyle Walker was penalised for an elbow on Fakhreddine Ben Youssef.

quote.citation: 2020 July 29, Ian Prosser discusses with Paul Stephen, “Rail needs robust and strategic plans”, in Rail, page 38:
quote.text: In the immediate term, there is a host of new operating procedures to be developed and to become familiarised with, in accordance with social distancing.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English host, oist, ost, from Old French hoiste, from Latin hostia (“sacrificial victim”). Doublet of hostie.

definitions.definition: (Christianity) The consecrated bread of the Eucharist.

quote.citation: 1978, John Lydon (lyrics and music), “Religion II”, performed by Public Image Ltd.:
quote.text: Do you pray to the Holy Ghost when you suck your host? / Do you read who's dead in the Irish Post?
